title: Across 37 countries, people more often expect AI to reduce jobs and widen inequality than to create broad economic opportunity
source_unit: Pew Research Center, Globally, More People Expect AI to Cause Job Loss Than Growth, 17 September 2026
geography: Adults in 36 countries surveyed in 2026, with comparisons across high- and middle-income countries and age, gender, income, education, ideology, and AI-awareness groups

observations.period: February 8-May 13, 2026; global expectations about AI and jobs

country_pattern.unit: number of 37 countries in which people tend to expect AI to lead to fewer rather than more jobs

high_income_job_loss.unit: median percent in 18 high-income countries saying AI will lead to fewer jobs in the next 20 years

middle_income_job_loss.unit: median percent in 18 middle-income countries saying AI will lead to fewer jobs

work-route.value: AI is entering public imagination as a labor-market redistribution problem before it is broadly accepted as a growth opportunity

observations.method: Pew Research Center international survey of nationally sampled adults across 36 countries, with the report’s 37-country comparisons incorporating U.S. survey data.
observations.uncertainty: These are expectations about a 20-year future, not forecasts or observed job losses; country medians conceal occupational, sectoral, and class differences.
observations.subgroup: Workers, young adults, older adults, high- and middle-income publics, people with different education and AI awareness, employers, and policymakers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower job-loss concern in some middle-income settings may reflect uncertainty or lower awareness rather than confidence that AI will create opportunity.

observations.period: 2026; AI, economic inequality, and development position

high_income_inequality.unit: median percent in high-income countries saying AI will increase the gap between rich and poor

middle_income_inequality.unit: median percent in middle-income countries saying AI will increase the gap

us_colombia_contrast.value: 46 percent in the U.S. versus 13 percent in Colombia say AI will increase the rich-poor gap

distribution_route.value: public expectations about AI’s distributive effects vary with national income, awareness, education, household income, and political ideology

observations.method: Pew cross-national comparison of perceived AI effects on economic inequality and subgroup differences.
observations.uncertainty: Attitudes about inequality do not estimate actual distributional effects or identify whether AI, policy, labor institutions, or market power will determine outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Higher- and lower-income households, educated and less-educated adults, left and right ideological groups, and populations in different development contexts.
observations.counterinterpretation: Different expectations may reflect different exposure, information, economic structures, or trust rather than disagreement about AI’s underlying capabilities.

denominator.unit: adult attitude percentage reference across 37 countries

concern.unit: median percent more concerned than excited about increased AI use in daily life

mixed_feeling.unit: median percent equally concerned and excited

excitement.unit: median percent more excited than concerned in high-income countries

awareness_route.value: AI awareness is associated with more differentiated and sometimes more optimistic views, while low awareness is more often paired with uncertainty or concern

observations.method: Pew survey comparison of concern, excitement, uncertainty, and AI awareness across countries and demographic groups.
observations.uncertainty: The relationship between awareness and optimism is correlational; awareness may reflect education, occupation, access, media, or prior experience.
observations.subgroup: Adults with different AI awareness, education, age, household income, and national technology exposure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Mixed concern and excitement may indicate active evaluation and openness to governance rather than simple rejection or adoption.

observations.period: 2024-2026; age and gender differences in AI expectations

young_adult_concern.value: in multiple countries, young adults are more likely than older adults to expect AI-related job loss; concern among U.S. adults ages 18-34 rose from 40 percent in 2024 to 55 percent in 2026

gender_gap.value: in 11 mostly high-income countries, women are more likely than men to expect fewer jobs from AI; in France the gap is 10 percentage points

political_gap.value: in the U.S., adults on the left are 31 points more likely than conservatives to say AI will increase inequality

open_test.value: connect AI attitudes to actual work transitions, bargaining power, training, regulation, and household security without treating expectations as outcomes

observations.method: Pew subgroup analysis by age, gender, ideology, education, household income, and awareness, including repeated U.S. measures.
observations.uncertainty: Subgroup differences describe attitudes and do not show which groups will experience job displacement, benefit from productivity, or gain political influence.
observations.subgroup: Young adults, older adults, women and men, ideological groups, workers, students, and households with unequal access to AI knowledge or protection.
observations.counterinterpretation: Greater concern can reflect higher awareness and engagement rather than greater vulnerability; younger adults may be more exposed to future labor-market change but not necessarily harmed.

related_sources.claim: Pew high-income-country analysis provides complementary development-position and AI-concern context.
Pew youth analysis provides complementary age-specific AI concern and job-expectation context.

boundary: This record adds a global AI-attitudes route from job-loss expectations and inequality concerns through awareness, age, gender, ideology, and possible labor-market governance. It uses public-opinion evidence, not realized job displacement, firm productivity, causal policy effects, respondent-level data in the corpus, or proof that pessimistic expectations become outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Pew Research Center report page was reviewed for the 36-country sample, 37-country comparison, job-loss and inequality medians, concern-excitement measures, age and gender patterns, repeated U.S. comparisons, and methodological boundaries.
